As with any discipline, science started out as philosophy (it was called Natural Philosophy). Why is the world the way it is? What makes this liquid behave the way it does? What are we breathing? Where are we? etc. Yes, through vigorous testing and data collection, we have found answers to many of life's questions. Absolutely not all of them. One of my parents is a physicists, and always taught me to question everything. It seems though whenever the unknown/questionable is brought up such as: Quantum vs Standard, the constants, human and non-human consciousness, dark matter, life on other planets, animal intelligence etc. The curious individual is instantly hit in the face with the bullshit of hive-mind-we-know-everything-don't-ask (reddit especially). What happened to the actual practice of science? (Being curious) We don't know everything, so shouldn't it be our place to ask the questions and discuss all of the possibilities? Cultures throughout history have "known" they were right, and then had their world turned upside down by theories they regarded as ridiculous. What makes us different? Albert Einstein gave most of the credit for his mathematical prowess to intuition and imagination, and yet, we base a completely logical system off of it. What? How? Why? I'm just saying, let's discuss the unknown more often. Maybe we'll find more answers, or ways in which to find the answers.
When did science become "it's not proven, so it can't be true."?

I think that language and money also have a huge effect on what is considered genuine, even when scientific tests and analysis have been conducted.

A language contains a culture's way of thinking, and although science crosses all boundaries as a way of testing, it is still limited by a culture's built-in taboos and biases when discussing possibilities and outcomes.

Money can pay for "answers" if a scientist is willing to take it in return for the manipulation of numbers. Take lead in gasoline for example; for years it was "safe" because one scientist was paid to say so. That is just a well-known example... Monsanto cough Agent Orange cough. If I were to go further on the subject of money in science, I might be called a conspiracy theorist.

If I believe in anything, it is the scientific method, and the ingenuity of the human mind.

I'm going to address both the points of your post and the comment you have made below here, just to save some space.

I believe that LandonTheWhite hit the nail on the head when he said "The most important thing is to be a skeptic but never a cynic." I don't believe that most of science and the scientific community has adopted the belief that if something isn't supported by fact it can't be true. The "we know everything" mentality is, I believe, a hallmark of bad science. Everyone knows that there are plenty of questions we still don't have answers to, and it is the job of scientists everywhere to seek answers to those questions.

That being said, there are certain hypotheses that have stood the test of time and rigorous experimenting long enough to become theories. If solid evidence against one of these theories were to be provided, it should be considered. But poking questions at these theories for the sake of poking questions leads to a point where time is being wasted. They have already withstood their questions and continued to stand time and time again. We have to say "job well done" at a certain point and move on to the other questions that need to be answered.

As for your comment, that's why skepticism is so important. It's necessary to be able to distinguish between good and bad science. If something is published in a peer-reviewed journal, it does not mean that it's infallible. You need to take the time to review the science for yourself; decide if the methodology of the experiment makes sense, see if you agree with the conclusions made by the authors or if there seems to be a flaw. Scientists are people, and people have their own interpretations of things and make mistakes. Yes, a peer-reviewed article should be viewed in a higher light than a blog post. But it's still important to actually understand what the article is saying, and how the authors arrived at their conclusions.
